Please read this carefully:

<document>
# Does a Shorter Working Week Raise Productivity? A Synthesis of Five Sources

*Evidence briefing. Prepared for a working group on working-time policy.*

## Purpose

This briefing weighs five pieces of evidence on whether reducing the working week by a fifth, with pay maintained, raises productivity: the Halden multi-organisation pilot (source 1), the Varden County randomised trial at nine months (source 2), a re-analysis of the Halden pilot (source 3), a meta-analysis of 23 studies (source 4), and the 24-month follow-up of the Varden trial and of 14 Halden organisations (source 5). It adds no new data. Its aim is to state what the five together support, at the strength they support it, and what they leave open.

## 1. What each source contributes, and how later sources qualify it

**Source 1** established that many organisations that volunteered could cut scheduled hours by 20% with little change in reported output, and reported a 23.4% gain in output per hour, gains in every sector, large falls in sickness and resignations, and 92% continuation. Taken alone, it suggests a large, general effect.

**Source 2** was the first randomised evidence, with record-based output and actual hours. It introduced the distinction that the rest of the body depends on: between discretionary work, where output can be produced at any time within a deadline, and coverage-bound work, where output depends on presence while demand arrives. Per actual hour, output rose 12.5% in case-processing and 6.7% in counter work; per employee it was roughly unchanged in the first and fell 11.4% in the second. It also showed that actual hours fall less than scheduled hours, and that dividing by scheduled hours inflated the case-processing estimate from 12.5% to 22%.

**Source 3** found that source 1's figures were inflated in several documented ways: seven of nine withdrawals occurred after the schedule began, mostly for workload reasons, not "during the preparation phase"; manager-reported output exceeded record-based output by 3.8 points; actual hours fell 14.1%, not 20%; and the 1.4% revenue rise was a real fall of about 2.6% after inflation of 4.1%. Correcting what could be corrected reduced the per-hour gain to 10.8% in a subset. These findings stand. Source 3 then went further, concluding that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact, attributing the remainder to novelty on the basis of an extrapolated survey trend, and dismissing source 2's meetings hypothesis as post hoc. Those further claims do not survive later evidence.

**Source 4** placed both studies in a wider literature. Its pooled per-hour estimate of 13.4% is inflated by the same features source 3 identified; the estimates from controlled designs (+8.2%), actual-hours studies (+7.9%), record-based studies (+9.7%), controlled discretionary studies (+9.6%) and bias adjustment (+9.1%) converge on roughly 8 to 10%. Its work-type moderator generalises source 2: per-worker output fell about 9% in coverage-bound settings, consistently, and was roughly maintained in discretionary ones. It rejected source 1's sector-general claim and source 3's artifact claim. Its own claim that effects show no decay was wrong, for the reason source 5 gives.

**Source 5** applied the strictest standards in the body: randomisation, record-based output, log-measured hours and a two-year horizon. The per-hour gain in case-processing declined from 12.5% to 8.5% (log hours) but remained clearly above zero. Output per employee stood at −3.4%, with a confidence interval including zero. A registered mediation test attributed 47% of the gain to fewer recurring meetings and 18% to reduced fatigue. Source 4's "no decay" conclusion rested on four long-follow-up studies, all uncontrolled and using scheduled hours. The counter arm was ended at month 12.

## 2. Weighing the estimates

**Table 1. Estimates of the change in output per hour, ordered by strength of design**

| Estimate | Source | Change per hour |
|---|---|---|
| Uncontrolled, manager-reported, scheduled hours | 1 | +23.4% |
| Uncontrolled survivors, records, actual hours, 24 months | 5 | +11.8% |
| Uncontrolled subset, records, actual hours, 6 months | 3 | +10.8% |
| Meta-analysis, all studies | 4 | +13.4% |
| Meta-analysis, bias-adjusted | 4 | +9.1% |
| Meta-analysis, controlled discretionary | 4 | +9.6% |
| Randomised, case-processing, 9 months, timesheets | 2 | +12.5% |
| Randomised, case-processing, 24 months, system logs | 5 | +8.5% |
| Randomised, counter work, 9 months | 2 | +6.7% |

Estimates fall as designs strengthen and stabilise around 8 to 10% for discretionary work. The figure of more than 20% is not supported by any design that measures actual hours.

## 3. What the body supports

Read as a whole, the five sources support a conditional answer.

1. **Per hour, yes, by a moderate amount.** In discretionary work, a 20% cut in scheduled hours raises output per actual hour by roughly 8 to 10% under controlled measurement, with some decline from the first year to the second but no sign of disappearing within two years. The headline figure of more than 20% is an artifact of scheduled-hours denominators, manager-reported output and selection.
2. **Per worker, no.** Because actual hours fall by 11 to 14%, not 20%, a per-hour gain of 8 to 10% roughly offsets the hours cut but does not exceed it. Output per worker in discretionary work is around 2 to 4% lower than it would have been, with intervals that include zero. "Same output in four days" is close to true there; "more output" is not supported.
3. **In coverage-bound work, the answer is no on any measure that matters to the people served.** Output per worker falls by about 9 to 11%, waits lengthen, and maintaining service requires about 12% more staff. Per-hour gains exist but are small. This is the most consistent finding in the body.
4. **About half the per-hour gain in the best-measured setting comes from removing recurring meetings**, a smaller part from reduced fatigue, and about a third is unexplained.
5. **Sickness absence and resignations fall substantially** in every source that measured them (by roughly 27 to 36% for sick days). These are real benefits, but they are not themselves productivity, and the body does not estimate how far they offset per-worker output losses.

Whether "productivity" rises therefore depends on whether it is measured per hour or per worker, and on whether output in a given role depends on presence. Both slogans, "a four-day week makes people more productive" and "the gains are a mirage", are wrong as stated.

## 4. What the body leaves open

- **Is the hours cut necessary for the gain?** About half the per-hour gain runs through cutting meetings. Two control offices that audited meetings without cutting hours saw a 4.1% per-hour rise, but that is two offices without a comparison group. No study had an arm that reorganised work without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone would capture much of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and last, is not settled by this body.
- **Beyond two years.** No controlled evidence extends past 24 months. The per-hour gain declined between 9 and 24 months; whether it stabilises or continues to decline is unknown.
- **The unexplained third** of the per-hour gain has no tested mechanism.
- **Manufacturing and shift production** are almost absent from the evidence (two studies, both mixed).
- **Private-sector controlled evidence** is thin; the strongest designs are in public administration.

## 5. Bottom line

A 20% cut in scheduled hours at full pay raises output per hour by roughly 8 to 10% in discretionary work, about half of it through fewer meetings, which roughly but not fully offsets the hours lost; in coverage-bound work it reduces output and service unless staff are added. Whether the gain requires the hours cut, or could be had by reorganising work alone, remains open.

</document>

# A Critical Reading of the Evidence Briefing on a Shorter Working Week

**This is a sound and mostly accurate synthesis, and its conditional bottom line is the right one.** It summarises each source fairly. It keeps the findings that held up separate from the claims that later evidence overturned. Its main conclusions match where I ended up after reviewing the five sources.

That match is worth flagging. The briefing reads as if it were built from the same chain of reasoning as my reviews, so my agreement shouldn't be taken as independent confirmation. Checked against the earlier caveats, it repeats one factual error, drops several qualifications, and states some conclusions more confidently than the evidence allows. For a policy working group, the dropped caveats are the main concern.

## Accuracy against the sources

Most figures are reproduced correctly. The problems:

**1. It repeats the mixed-measure comparison.**
Section 1 says the case-processing gain "declined from 12.5% to 8.5% (log hours)". The 12.5% was measured with timesheets and the 8.5% with system logs. On a consistent basis (timesheets at both points), the decline was from 12.5% to 9.8%. Mixing the two overstates the fall: about 32% instead of about 22%.

**2. It describes the decline without the contamination caveat.**
Two control offices cut their meetings at month 15. That improved the control group and narrowed the measured gap, so part of the apparent decline may come from the control side rather than from fading. The decline should be described as "some decline, possibly overstated".

**3. "Its own claim that effects show no decay was wrong" goes too far.**
Source 5 showed that the meta-analysis's no-decay claim was unsupported, because it rested only on uncontrolled studies using scheduled hours. One controlled study showing a partly confounded decline doesn't establish that the claim was wrong.

**4. Table 1 is not ordered as claimed, and doesn't show what the text says it shows.**
- **The ordering.** The pooled meta-analysis estimate (+13.4%) sits below two uncontrolled subsets. The counter-work estimate is a different kind of work, placed on the same ranking.
- **The trend.** The text says "estimates fall as designs strengthen". But the randomised nine-month estimate (+12.5%) is higher than both uncontrolled corrected subsets (+10.8% and +11.8%).
- **What the table actually shows.** Correcting the hours and output measures matters a lot, and follow-up length matters somewhat. Randomisation alone doesn't pull the estimates down in a neat sequence.
- **The fix.** Separate discretionary from coverage-bound estimates and order the rows by which corrections each one applies.

**5. "Same output in four days is close to true" misdescribes what happened.**
Staff worked about 33–34 hours a week, which is more than four 8-hour days. That includes work on the day off and claimed overtime. The accurate statement is "about 3% less output from about 11% fewer actual hours". The slogan implies the scheduled cut was achieved; it wasn't.

## What the briefing does well

- **It handles the critiques fairly.** It accepts Source 3's documented corrections while rejecting its "entirely an artifact" conclusion.
- **It separates per-hour from per-worker productivity** and recognises that this distinction drives most of the disagreement in the debate.
- **It identifies the coverage-bound finding as the most consistent result** in the body of evidence, which it is.
- **Its open questions are the right ones.** The most important is whether cutting hours is necessary for the gain, or whether reorganising work alone would do.
- **It rejects both slogans**, "more productive" and "a mirage", for good reasons.

## What it drops or overstates

**1. The sources are less independent than "five sources" suggests.**
- There are really two primary datasets (Halden and Varden), plus a meta-analysis that includes both, plus two re-analyses or follow-ups of those same datasets.
- Halden figures appear in four of the five sources.
- Source 5 was written by Source 2's authors together with Source 1's lead author.

Agreement across the "five sources" is therefore partly circular. A working group should understand that the strongest discretionary-work evidence comes from 14 offices in one public employer.

**2. The 8–10% range sounds more precise than it is.**
- **The best estimate is uncertain.** It has a 95% confidence interval of +3.4% to +13.8%.
- **That interval is probably too narrow.** It is calculated from very few clusters, and no small-sample correction was reported.
- **The "convergence" overlaps.** The meta-analysis subgroups draw largely on the same studies, and none applies every correction at once, so the 8–10% may be an upper bound.

A more honest summary would be "probably in the mid-to-high single digits, plausibly anywhere from about 3% to 14%".

**3. The meetings finding is generalised beyond its evidence.**
Section 3 correctly limits it to "the best-measured setting". The bottom line then states it as a general fact about discretionary work: "about half of it through fewer meetings". It actually rests on one mediation analysis in one employer, with these unresolved issues:
- only 14 offices;
- possible reverse causation, since meeting time and output were measured over the same period;
- uncertainty about whether log-measured hours include meeting time;
- a confidence interval running from 28% to 66%.

**4. The sickness figures may be partly mechanical.**
The briefing calls 27–36% falls in sick days "real benefits". None of the sources say whether staff moved to four-day rotas. If they did, counting sick days over fewer working days would reduce the totals regardless of any change in health. The fall should be measured as sick time as a share of scheduled time. Until then, the size of the benefit is uncertain, though some real benefit is plausible. The Varden resignation estimates are also described in that trial as imprecise.

**5. There is no cost estimate, though policy decisions depend on one.**
- **Discretionary work:** output per employee falls about 3.4% at unchanged pay, so cost per unit of output rises about 3.5%, plus any paid overtime.
- **Coverage-bound work:** keeping service at the same level raised cost per contact by about 9% in Varden.

These are the most decision-relevant numbers in the evidence, and the briefing leaves them out. It also doesn't say how much, if anything, lower sickness and turnover might offset the higher costs.

**6. The reversion evidence is left out.**
The briefing never mentions that organisations went back to normal hours:
- 5 of 61 Halden organisations, all in retail, hospitality and healthcare administration;
- 3 of the 14 followed up for 24 months, including a marketing agency citing client deadlines.

The marketing agency is discretionary work in which reduced hours still failed. That suggests a third category: discretionary work tied to client deadlines. The simple discretionary/coverage-bound split doesn't capture it.

**7. Some quality and service gaps aren't listed as open questions.**
- **Backlogs.** Backlog levels and compliance with statutory deadlines were never reported, even though they were raised as concerns.
- **Quality.** The only quality measure for case-processing, appeal overturn rates, is insensitive.
- **Counter productivity.** The per-hour gain at counters may reflect staff being busier with longer queues, rather than working more efficiently.
- **Attrition.** Source 3 documented attrition in the Halden pilot but never corrected for it.

## Suggested revised bottom line

> In discretionary work, cutting scheduled hours by 20% at full pay reduces actual hours by about 11–14% and raises output per actual hour by an uncertain amount, best estimated in the high single digits. That estimate comes mainly from one public employer and lasts at least two years with some decline. Output per worker falls slightly (about 2–4%), so cost per unit of output rises modestly. In the one setting tested, much of the gain came from cutting recurring meetings, and it is unknown whether that requires the hours cut. In coverage-bound work, and in some client-deadline work, reduced hours cut output and service unless more staff are hired, at roughly 9% higher cost per unit in the one costed case. Falls in sickness absence and resignations are consistent across sources, but their size may be partly a counting effect.

The briefing's structure and judgement are sound. Correcting the decline figure and Table 1, restoring the dropped caveats, and adding costs would make it reliable enough for a working group to act on.
